Meaning: The study of how individuals and society make choices when resources are limited.
Example: Because resources are limited, we cannot satisfy every want.

Meaning: Resources are limited, but human wants are not.
Example: Scarcity means choices must be made about how resources are allocated.
Trap: THE starting point of the whole subject: scarcity → choice → trade-off.

Meaning: Choosing more of one thing usually means giving up something else.
Example: A student trades off study against leisure.

Meaning: The value of the next-best alternative you give up when making a choice.
Example: Study for a Master's instead of working: the opportunity cost includes the income you gave up.
Trap: Not always money. Time and other alternatives count too.

Meaning: The resources used to produce things: land, labour and capital.
Example: Land, labour and capital are the three factors.

Meaning: Natural resources used in production.
Example: Land, oil, minerals and water.

Meaning: Human physical and mental effort used in production.
Example: Workers, managers and designers.

Meaning: Equipment and structures used to produce goods and services.
Example: Machines, factories and technology.
Trap: In IC103 capital = physical equipment (K). In IC101 it meant money. Different meaning.

Meaning: To decide where resources should go.
Example: Scarcity means choices must be made about how resources are allocated.

Meaning: Getting the most from available resources.
Example: Efficiency is about the size of the cake.

Meaning: How resources and outcomes are distributed.
Example: Equity is about how the cake is shared.
Trap: In IC103 equity = fairness. In IC101 equity = ownership of a company. Totally different.

Meaning: The benefit from one additional unit.
Example: Do more when marginal benefit is greater than marginal cost.

Meaning: The cost of one additional unit.
Example: An airline asks: what is the extra cost of selling one more seat?

Meaning: To decide by comparing the cost and benefit of ONE more unit, not the total.
Example: Should the airline sell the last empty seat at a discount?
Trap: "Marginal" always means "one more unit". It is the most used word in the module.

Meaning: Something that encourages people to act in a certain way.
Example: Prices are incentives: a higher price discourages buyers but encourages sellers.

Meaning: Adam Smith's idea that buyers and sellers pursuing their own interests can coordinate the economy without central direction.
Example: Separate decisions can help coordinate economic activity.

Meaning: The study of individual consumers, firms and markets.
Example: Why does quantity demanded fall when price rises?

Meaning: The study of the economy as a whole.
Example: Why does inflation rise? What causes unemployment?

Meaning: Holding all other things constant.
Example: Ceteris paribus, when price rises, quantity demanded falls.
Trap: Latin for "other things equal". It appears in almost every definition.

Meaning: A group of buyers and sellers of a particular good or service.
Example: Local food markets or online marketplaces.

Meaning: How much consumers are willing and able to buy at different prices.
Example: Demand is the buyers' side of the market.

Meaning: How much producers are willing and able to sell at different prices.
Example: Supply is the sellers' side of the market.

Meaning: Ceteris paribus, price and quantity demanded move in OPPOSITE directions.
Example: When price rises, quantity demanded falls.

Meaning: Ceteris paribus, price and quantity supplied move in the SAME direction.
Example: When price rises, quantity supplied rises.

Meaning: The amount consumers are willing and able to buy AT A PARTICULAR PRICE.
Example: At 50p per kg, market quantity demanded is 700,000 tonnes.
Trap: THE exam trap: a price fall raises QUANTITY DEMANDED, it does not "increase demand".

Meaning: The amount sellers are willing and able to sell AT A PARTICULAR PRICE.
Example: A higher price raises quantity supplied.
Trap: Same trap as quantity demanded. Price change ≠ change in supply.

Meaning: A table of prices and the quantity demanded at each one.
Example: The demand schedule becomes the demand curve.

Meaning: A downward-sloping line showing quantity demanded at each price.
Example: Price on the vertical axis, quantity on the horizontal axis.

Meaning: An upward-sloping line showing quantity supplied at each price.
Example: The supply curve slopes upward.

Meaning: A change caused by the good's OWN price. It changes quantity demanded/supplied.
Example: Own-price change → movement along the curve.
Trap: THE most examined distinction in Lecture 1. Own price = movement.

Meaning: A change caused by ANY OTHER determinant. It changes demand/supply itself.
Example: A rise in income shifts the whole demand curve.
Trap: Anything except own price = shift.

Meaning: A good you buy MORE of when your income rises.
Example: Income up → demand for a normal good up.

Meaning: A good you buy LESS of when your income rises.
Example: It does not mean bad quality. It means you switch away as you get richer.
Trap: NOT "bad quality". Only about how demand responds to income.

Meaning: Goods you can use instead of each other.
Example: Price of coffee up → demand for tea up.

Meaning: Goods used together.
Example: Price of printers up → demand for ink down.

Meaning: Where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied.
Example: At equilibrium there is no pressure for price to change.

Meaning: The price at which buyers want to buy exactly what sellers want to sell.
Example: Set demand equal to supply and solve.

Meaning: To have no unsold goods and no unmet demand.
Example: The market clears at equilibrium.

Meaning: Quantity supplied is greater than quantity demanded. Price is ABOVE equilibrium.
Example: Sellers cannot sell everything, so price tends to fall.

Meaning: Quantity demanded is greater than quantity supplied. Price is BELOW equilibrium.
Example: Consumers want more than firms are selling, so price tends to rise.

Meaning: A measure of how much buyers and sellers respond to a change in market conditions.
Example: Elasticity tells us how sensitive demand is to a change in price.

Meaning: The responsiveness of quantity demanded to a change in price. % change in Qd ÷ % change in P.
Example: PED is normally negative because demand curves slope down.
Trap: Normally NEGATIVE, but we discuss the absolute value.

Meaning: |PED| greater than 1: quantity responds MORE than proportionally to price.
Example: Luxuries are usually elastic.

Meaning: |PED| less than 1: quantity responds LESS than proportionally to price.
Example: Necessities are usually inelastic.

Meaning: |PED| equals 1: the percentage changes are exactly the same.
Example: Total revenue stays the same.

Meaning: A vertical demand curve: quantity does not change at all when price changes.
Example: If price rises, consumers buy exactly the same quantity.

Meaning: A horizontal demand curve: a tiny price rise sends quantity demanded to zero.
Example: This is the demand curve a perfectly competitive firm faces.

Meaning: Elasticity measured BETWEEN two points, using the average of the two as the base.
Example: It gives the same answer in both directions: A to B and B to A.
Trap: Invented to fix the problem that A→B and B→A gave different answers (-0.66 vs -1.5).

Meaning: Elasticity at a SINGLE point, using the derivative of the demand function.
Example: At a single point the change is infinitesimally small.

Meaning: What makes demand elastic: close substitutes, and whether it is a luxury or a necessity.
Example: The easier a good is to avoid or replace, the more elastic demand is.

Meaning: How quantity demanded responds to a change in income.
Example: Normal goods positive; inferior goods negative.

Meaning: How demand for one good responds to the price of ANOTHER good.
Example: Substitutes positive; complements negative.
Trap: The SIGN tells you the relationship. Positive = substitutes.

Meaning: How responsive quantity supplied is to a change in price. Always positive.
Example: Supply is more elastic in the long run, because producers have time to adjust.

Meaning: Price times quantity sold. The same number as total consumer expenditure.
Example: TR = P × Q.
Trap: If demand is ELASTIC, a price cut RAISES total revenue. Classic MCQ.

Meaning: The amount consumers spend on a good. Equals the firms' total revenue.
Example: It is the area of the rectangle formed by price and quantity.

Meaning: The satisfaction a consumer gets from consuming a good or service.
Example: Rational consumers choose to maximise their utility.

Meaning: The total satisfaction from all units consumed in a period.
Example: TU rises as you consume more, but more and more slowly.

Meaning: The additional satisfaction from consuming ONE extra unit.
Example: MU = ΔTU / ΔQ.

Meaning: The more of a product you consume, the less extra satisfaction each new unit gives.
Example: The fifth packet of crisps gives less pleasure than the first.
Trap: This is WHY the demand curve slopes down.

Meaning: The maximum a consumer will pay for a good. The monetary value of utility.
Example: The demand curve can be read as consumers' willingness to pay.

Meaning: The difference between what a consumer WOULD pay and what they ACTUALLY pay.
Example: Consumer surplus is the gain from trade for the buyer.

Meaning: MU minus price, for one more unit.
Example: At the optimum, MCS of the last unit is zero.

Meaning: Consumers maximise utility by making marginal utility per £1 equal across all goods.
Example: MU_a / P_a = MU_b / P_b.
Trap: Guaranteed exam formula. Equal MU per pound, not equal MU.

Meaning: All combinations of two goods that give the consumer the SAME satisfaction.
Example: The consumer is indifferent between any two points on the same curve.

Meaning: The slope of the indifference curve: the rate at which you will swap one good for the other.
Example: MRS usually diminishes as you move along the curve.

Meaning: A set of indifference curves. Higher curves mean higher satisfaction.
Example: Two indifference curves can never intersect.
Trap: Why can they never cross? Because it would mean two different utility levels at one point.

Meaning: All combinations of two goods the consumer can afford, given income and prices.
Example: A change in income shifts it in parallel; a price change rotates it.
Trap: Income change = PARALLEL SHIFT. Price change = ROTATION.

Meaning: Where the budget line is TANGENT to the highest reachable indifference curve.
Example: The consumer chooses the highest curve the budget allows.

Meaning: How the chosen combination changes as INCOME changes.
Example: It traces the optimal points as the budget line shifts outward.

Meaning: How the chosen combination changes as the PRICE of one good changes.
Example: Plotting these gives you the demand curve.

Meaning: The change in consumption because the good became relatively more expensive.
Example: Coffee gets dearer, so you switch to tea.
Trap: ALWAYS negative: price up → consumption down. No exceptions.

Meaning: The change in consumption because a price change altered your real purchasing power.
Example: A price rise makes you effectively poorer.
Trap: Negative for a NORMAL good, POSITIVE for an inferior good. This is the key pair.

Meaning: What your money can actually buy.
Example: Income has not changed, but the same money now buys less.

Meaning: The assumption that a firm aims to maximise profit.
Example: Profit = total revenue − total cost.

Meaning: An input that cannot be changed in the short run.
Example: Capital (machinery) is usually fixed in the short run.

Meaning: An input that CAN be changed.
Example: Labour is usually the variable input.

Meaning: A period in which at least one factor is FIXED.
Example: In the short run, capital K is constant.
Trap: The short run is defined by fixed factors, NOT by calendar time.

Meaning: A period in which ALL factors are variable.
Example: In the long run, both L and K can change.

Meaning: The relationship showing how inputs produce output. Q = f(L, K).
Example: L is labour, K is capital.

Meaning: The total output produced from a given amount of inputs.
Example: TPP rises, then flattens, and can eventually fall.

Meaning: Output per unit of the variable input. APP = TPP / L.
Example: Output per worker.
Trap: APP rises while MPP is ABOVE it, and falls while MPP is below it.

Meaning: The extra output from ONE more unit of the variable input. MPP = ΔTPP / ΔL.
Example: MPP is the slope of the TPP curve.
Trap: TPP is at its MAXIMUM when MPP = 0. Exam favourite.

Meaning: Adding more of a variable input to a FIXED input eventually gives less and less extra output.
Example: Too many baristas, one coffee machine.
Trap: Sets in when MPP starts to FALL, which is BEFORE total output starts to fall.

Meaning: A payment actually made to an outside supplier.
Example: Wages and rent are explicit costs.

Meaning: A cost with no payment, but a sacrifice of an alternative.
Example: The salary the owner gave up to run the business.

Meaning: Cost that does not change with output.
Example: Rent stays at £12 whatever you produce.

Meaning: Cost that changes with output.
Example: Materials and wages rise as you produce more.

Meaning: TC = TFC + TVC.
Example: Total cost is fixed plus variable cost.

Meaning: A cost already spent that cannot be recovered.
Example: Sunk costs should not affect your next decision.

Meaning: AFC = TFC / Q.
Example: AFC always falls as output rises, because the fixed cost is spread wider.

Meaning: AVC = TVC / Q.
Example: Average variable cost per unit.

Meaning: Total cost per unit. AC = TC / Q = AFC + AVC.
Example: AC is U-shaped.

Meaning: The extra cost of producing ONE more unit. MC = ΔTC / ΔQ.
Example: All marginal costs are variable, because fixed costs do not change.
Trap: MC cuts AC and AVC at their MINIMUM points. Guaranteed diagram question.

Meaning: MC is at its MINIMUM exactly where MPP is at its MAXIMUM.
Example: They are mirror images of each other.

Meaning: What happens to output when ALL inputs rise by the same percentage.
Example: Increasing, constant or decreasing returns.

Meaning: An x% rise in inputs gives MORE than x% more output.
Example: Inputs up 10%, output up 15%.

Meaning: An x% rise in inputs gives exactly x% more output.
Example: Inputs up 10%, output up 10%.

Meaning: An x% rise in inputs gives LESS than x% more output.
Example: Inputs up 10%, output up 6%.

Meaning: Increasing the SCALE of production lowers the cost per unit.
Example: Specialisation, indivisibilities, efficiency of a large plant.
Trap: Economies of SCALE = one product, bigger. Economies of SCOPE = more products.

Meaning: Increasing the scale RAISES the cost per unit.
Example: Usually from problems of management and coordination.

Meaning: Producing a wider RANGE of products lowers the cost of each.
Example: Sharing overheads between product lines.

Meaning: Total cost per unit in the long run, when all inputs can change.
Example: The LRAC curve shows economies, then constant costs, then diseconomies.

Meaning: The extra cost of one more unit in the long run.
Example: LRMC cuts LRAC at its minimum.

Meaning: Revenue per unit sold. AR = TR / Q. It is the same as price.
Example: AR is the demand curve the firm faces.
Trap: AR = Price. Always. The AR curve IS the firm's demand curve.

Meaning: The extra revenue from selling ONE more unit. MR = ΔTR / ΔQ.
Example: For a price taker, MR = AR = P.

Meaning: A firm that must accept the market price and cannot set its own.
Example: In perfect competition, P = AR = MR.

Meaning: Producing where MR = MC.
Example: Stage 1: find output where MR = MC. Stage 2: measure profit with AR and AC.
Trap: The two-stage method. Stage 1 finds QUANTITY, stage 2 finds PROFIT.

Meaning: How a market is organised: number of firms, entry barriers, product type, competition.
Example: It affects how firms behave.

Meaning: The combined market share of the largest firms in an industry.
Example: The five-firm ratio for motor vehicles (63.86) is far above food products (10.68).

Meaning: A firm's ability to affect the price or market conditions.
Example: Firms in perfect competition have almost no market power.

Meaning: Many small firms, identical products, free entry, perfect information, and firms are price takers.
Example: Agriculture is the usual example.

Meaning: Products that buyers see as identical.
Example: Wheat from one farm is the same as from another.

Meaning: Products that are similar but not the same.
Example: Restaurants differ by menu and atmosphere.

Meaning: Buyers and sellers know all prices and product details.
Example: It is an assumption of perfect competition.

Meaning: New firms can enter the market easily and leave easily.
Example: Free entry drives supernormal profit down over time.

Meaning: The profit level where ECONOMIC profit is zero. Revenue covers all costs including opportunity cost.
Example: In long-run perfect competition, firms earn only normal profit.
Trap: Normal profit is NOT zero profit. It means zero ECONOMIC profit. Biggest trap here.

Meaning: Profit ABOVE normal profit. Revenue exceeds all costs including opportunity cost.
Example: Supernormal profits attract new firms into the market.

Meaning: Profit after ALL costs, including opportunity cost.
Example: Normal profit means economic profit = 0.

Meaning: Choosing output to make losses as small as possible, when profit is negative.
Example: It still uses the MR = MC rule.

Meaning: A stable position where firms earn only normal profit and nobody enters or leaves.
Example: P = AR = MR = MC = AC = LRAC at its minimum.
Trap: Memorise the chain: P = AR = MR = MC = AC. Appears as a gap-fill.

Meaning: A market with a SINGLE seller.
Example: A local water company.

Meaning: The single firm that sells in a monopoly market.
Example: A monopolist faces the whole market demand curve.

Meaning: Things that make it hard for new firms to enter a market.
Example: They are the fundamental cause of monopoly.

Meaning: Barriers that come from the nature of the industry itself.
Example: Starting the business may need an enormous investment.

Meaning: Barriers a firm creates deliberately to block rivals.
Example: An exclusive contract that stops rivals reaching key distributors.

Meaning: One large firm can supply the market at a lower average cost than several small ones.
Example: It comes from large economies of scale.

Meaning: One firm controls an essential input that rivals need.
Example: De Beers and the supply of diamonds.

Meaning: A legal right stopping others from making or selling an invention for a time.
Example: Patents prevent competitors producing the same product.

Meaning: To sell more, the monopolist must LOWER the price.
Example: This is why MR lies BELOW AR for a monopoly.
Trap: For a monopoly MR < AR. For a price taker MR = AR. Know the difference.

Meaning: When a firm does not produce at the lowest possible cost, because competition is weak.
Example: A monopoly may show X-inefficiency.

Meaning: Many firms, free entry, but DIFFERENTIATED products.
Example: Restaurants and hairdressers.

Meaning: A market dominated by a FEW large firms.
Example: Airlines, supermarkets and mobile networks.
